prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
repeatability: May be taken three times for credit.

title: Classical Archaeology
description: History of the discipline through the individuals, organizations, excavations, theoretical models and ethical issues that have shaped it.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: CLAS 444/ANTH 444 .

title: Studies in Africa and the African Diaspora
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the history of Africa and its global diasporas through the perspective of archaeology and related fields. Examines prehistoric African cultures, ancient civilizations and pre-Atlantic trade and exchange networks. Explores the nature of the transatlantic trade and the creation of the African Diaspora in the Americas and the Caribbean. Explores the cultural identities of African-descended communities in the Americas and other regions of the world. Applies interdisciplinary research methods that combine historical, archaeological and ethnographic case studies to challenge colonial narratives about Africa and its diasporas. Uses hands-on work with material culture and related evidence to highlight archaeology’s role in understanding the histories and cultures of Africa and its diasporas. TOPICS AND THEMES. African prehistory and civilizations, West Africa before Europe, Africa and its global diasporas, Atlantic Africa and the creation of the African diaspora, African cultural resilience, adaptation, and hybridity in the African diaspora, landscapes of power and resistance, material culture, memory, heritage and social justice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

title: Lithic Artifact Analysis
description: Laboratory-based course reviewing methods archaeologists use to analyze stone tools and debitage, including identification of tool-stone sources, reconstruction of technology, explanation of assemblage variability, and microscopic use-wear analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ANTH 202 and approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

title: Quantitative Methods in Anthropology
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Presents practical training in statistics applicable to anthropological and archaeological data. Provides anthropology students with the sophisticated statistical skills needed for an increasingly quantitative field. Discusses reasons why anthropological and archaeological data does not always meet the criteria set by many formal statistical models. Teaches the methods to analyze the chronological, geographic, morphometric, demographic, phylogenetic, genetic, linguistic, network/interaction and observational datasets (among others) that pose unique challenges for both analysis and interpretation. Conducts scientific statistical analyses of these datasets. Applies statistical concepts and techniques to real and hypothetical anthropological or archaeological problems during weekly lab sections. TOPICS AND THEMES. Quantitative analytical methods employed by anthropologists; includes statistical analyses, statistical software and sampling theory commonly used in anthropological research. Graphical techniques and statistics specific to anthropological datasets and research questions, including exploratory data analysis (e.g. principal components, canonical variates, factor analysis), and other multivariate methods (e.g. MANOVA). This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; STAT 302 or STAT 303 .

title: The Archaeology and Anthropology of Foraging Societies
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology and anthropology of foraging (hunting and gathering) societies in time and space. Includes an overview of archaeology focused on foraging societies and current methodological and theoretical issues, especially the use of ethnographic and environmental data. Investigates ecologically oriented case studies of late Pleistocene and Holocene hunter-gatherers paired with the ethnographic record used to interpret these sites. Archaeological case studies will have an emphasis on land-use, site-structure and site formation analyses. Ethnographic case studies will focus on the diversity of hunting and gathering societies, change in these societies through time and discussion of forager economies, with specific attention to critiquing ethnohistoric accounts and the applicability of these case studies to the archaeological record. TOPICS AND THEMES. Forager (hunter-gatherer) variation in different environments; forager variation through time; forager social structures; forager mobility; forager subsistence; socio-political complexity in foraging societies; ethnographic critiques; archaeology of foraging societies; resource management; foragers in the modern world and change in forager societies in the recent past; archaeological site structure; lithic analysis; site formation processes; archaeological site survey; archaeological theory of foragers; site modeling and resource modeling. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

title: Quantitative Ethnographic Methods
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces quantitative ethnographic field methods commonly used in anthropological research to formally test hypotheses. Explores the benefits and challenges of applying structured, quantitative techniques to the study of complex cultural phenomena within a field largely dominated by qualitative methods. Covers best practices for managing and analyzing anthropological datasets. Surveys common ethnographic methods designed to enhance comparability and analytical rigor of ethnographic research, including structured interviews, text analysis and network analysis. Through hands-on assignments, provides practical experience in developing and executing small-scale research projects. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include ethical considerations in field research, research design, data management, statistical analysis, structured interviews, online survey tools, standardized observation, network analysis, text analysis and cultural consensus analysis. Also includes student participation in all stages of the research process, including research design, data collection, data management and analysis, and write-up.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

title: Environmental Archaeology
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the paleoecological context in which past humans interacted with the natural environment encompassing plants, animals and landscape. Introduces students to theories and methods relevant to studying past human-environment interactions. Outlines types of environmental data that survive in the archaeological record (geological, botanical, faunal, chemical), recovery and analytical methods, absolute chronology and inferences made based on these data. Develops long-term, global perspective on human-environment interactions provided by the fields of archaeology and earth science. TOPICS AND THEMES. The use of archaeological sites as paleoenvironmental archives, human impacts on ancient environments, Quaternary extinctions, long-term landscape evolution, plant and animal domestication, the Anthropocene and cultural collapse and resilience.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ANTH 202 , ANTH 204 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

title: Method and Theory in the Peopling of the Americas
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Reviews current evidence from the fields of archaeology, genetics, biological anthropology and paleoecology for the dispersal of modern humans to the New World during the Pleistocene. Examines terminal Pleistocene cultures in Asia and the earliest sites in the Americas. Discusses various models proposed for this migration. Critically examines major archaeological sites and cultures. Stresses an interdisciplinary approach. Applies theory and method used to explain prehistoric human migration and colonization of empty lands. TOPICS AND THEMES. Pleistocene Americas; ancient DNA; paleoenvironments; radiocarbon dating; archaeological modeling; lithic analysis; ethnographic analogy; zooarchaeology and extinctions; archaeological site formation processes; critical analysis of fragmentary data; statistical analysis. This course will incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to the peopling of the Americas. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ANTH 202 or ANTH 204 and approval of instructor.

title: Cultural Heritage and Resource Management
description: Evaluation of modern ideas about how and why archaeological, architectural, ethnographic, and natural resources should be preserved and presented to current and future societies; critical examination of the theories, methods, regulations, and ethics that guide efforts to preserve and protect cultural heritage within a context of past endeavors and future directions.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Ancient Biomolecules
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how biomolecules — DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites — persist in plant and animal remains, artifacts and sediments for thousands to millions of years, preserving key insights into long-term ecological and human history. Determines how these molecules are preserved, identified and analyzed within archaeological contexts to address interdisciplinary questions about evolution, migration, diet, disease, culture, tool production, health and environmental change. Interpretation of biomolecular evidence will draw from archaeological, historical and scientific sources to reconstruct past lifeways within their own cultural and environmental settings. Develops the ability through lectures, discussions and data analysis to assess the suitability for different biomolecular methods for addressing specific research questions and critically evaluate current scientific literature in the field. Skills learned are directly applicable to making informed, evidence-based decisions, empowering students to navigate information-rich environments with discernment and confidence. Prior knowledge in either biology/biochemistry or archaeology is required, but not both. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of the hereditary biomolecules DNA, proteins, lipids and metabolites; large-scale ‘omics’ approaches, including genomics, metagenomics, proteomics, metaproteomics, lipiomics and metabolomics used to investigate complex systems; instrumentation including PCR, Sanger sequencing, whole genome sequencing (NGS and WGS), chromatography and mass spectrometry; specialized applications such as environmental DNA, microbiomes and dental calculus genetics and proteomics; biomolecule preservation and degradation; ways biomolecular techniques are adapted for archaeological considerations; integration with other lines of archaeological, textual, historic and scientific evidence. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to archaeological biomolecules.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ANTH 202 or BIOL 111 , or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

title: Anthropology of Body Image
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Evaluates core psychological, medical, evolutionary and anthropological theories of body image, eating disorders, fat and cosmetic surgery. Surveys and critiques theories of body image from the lens of medical anthropology and global mental health. Develops expertise in articulating the major theoretical questions, strengths and limitations of different frameworks, particularly in relation to cross-cultural variation. Critically analyzes global case studies of body image-related illnesses. Applies anthropological theories to identifying biases in the body image literature and public health consequences. Formulates anthropological solutions to conversations and concerns in the body image literature surrounding emerging trends, cross-cultural value- and knowledge-systems, and the challenges of treatment. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analysis of anthropological theories of the body; critique of current theories of body image and eating disorders; assessment of psychological and anthropological approaches to fat talk; critique and synthesis of biomedical and social justice approaches to weight and weight stigma; evaluation of limitations of eating disorders research from a cross-cultural perspective; formulation of anthropological solutions to emerging discussions in body image among men, racial minorities and sexual minorities; evaluating the cross-cultural motivations and ethics of cosmetic surgery; critiquing current treatments for eating disorders and obesity from an anthropological lens.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

title: Anthropology Internship
description: Provides students with the opportunity to gain practical experience in a variety of settings, including local, state or federal agencies; museums; non-profit organizations; non-governmental organizations; private firms. May be taken four times for credit.

description: For individual research in anthropology on subjects not included in established courses. May be repeated for credit.
